# Draft:Edward S. Hynes

Edward S. Hynes
Born: Edward Sylvester Hynes
Date: 3 June 1897
Place: Nottingham, Nottinghamshire, England (Public records: Volume 7b Page 345)
Died: 12 May 1982 in Newquay, Burren, Co. Clare and is buried at Corcomroe Abbey, County Clare
Unmarried; no children
Edward Sylvester Hynes (3 June 1897) was an artist best known for his work as a caricaturist and political cartoonist.
Early life and education
Born on 3 June 1897 in Nottingham, U.K., the seventh of eight children, Edward was named after his father, Edward Charles Hynes MD of Bayfield, Burren County Clare. His mother was Alicia Mary Josephine Willis daughter of Robert Willis MD of Wellpark House, Oughterard, County Galway.
His early years were spent at 54 Shakespeare Street, Nottingham according to the 1901 and 1911 United Kingdom Census. As the younger son of a large family, he was sent to sea. In 1917, he enrolled in the Marine School of South Shields as Second Mate and then served in the Merchant Navy as navigating officer.
He later enrolled at Sheffield University to study medicine but after 3 years he returned to his naval career.
Career
After 10 years at sea the post-war slump led him to London. There his artistic talent was noticed when he drew a caricature of the then Earl Beatty. This opened up new opportunities for him.
His works were first published in Town Topics (edited W. Buchanan-Taylor) and soon he was collaborating with magazines such as The Bystander, Illustrated Sporting and Dramatic News. By 1924 he was a regular contributor to several magazines.
My Method
by THE LEADING EUROPEAN BLACK AND WHITE ARTISTS.
In 1926, Hynes was one of the 5 British artists to contribute to "My Method by the Leading European Black and White Artists" published by Gordon & Gotch Ltd., London. The preface states the importance of understanding the thought process leading to specific styles of drawing.
Hynes describes the art form he has chosen and his humour is visible: “paraphernalia …won’t hinder your work. But it will certainly not make you into a successful caricaturist ...You might as well give an infant a slide rule and expect him to show that he is an engineer”. A clear message: Caricaturing is not for everybody. For Hynes being an artist is the ability to make something unusual and working to develop an individual style.
His article in this book is the basis upon which he later based the “Lesson 14”: Caricaturing Humorous Drawing and Cartooning for the British & Dominions School of Drawing Ltd. London. .
He continued to contribute to The Bystander, The Daily Sketch, The Evening News, Gentlewoman, Humourist, Illustrated Sporting and Dramatic News, Lilliput, London Calling, London Opinion, Men Only, Night & Day, Razzle, The Strand Magazine, Sunday Express (especially during WW2), Tatler and Town Topics. Hynes was often quoted as a feature artist in advertisements for the newspapers and magazines his works were published in. His cartoons were used to illustrate short stories in magazines as well as series for example “if gossip we must” (the Bystander), “Celebrities in Cameo” (The Bystander); “The Stage of the Day” (The Illustrated and Dramatic News); “Our Captious Critic”, (The Illustrated and Dramatic News) as well as in books such as “Dancing Through the Ages”, (Royal Palace Hotel, Kensington).
Edward also worked in advertising producing works for Mex petrol, Wright’s Coal Tar Shaving Cream, J. Lyons, Guiness, Player’s Tobacco among others.
His career evolved and was commented on in the printed press of the time: “Hynes…a recent recruit to the ranks of leading London caricaturists, but his brilliant work as the “Captious Critic” artist in The Illustrated Sporting and Dramatic News has placed him quickly in the front rank of the comic illustrators of the press” The Illustrated Sporting and Dramatic News ; “eminent artist” The Scotsman , “a humourist artist who is known throughout the world for his keen sense of the ridiculous”, The Berwickshire News; “that prosperous-looking gentleman who is Hynes, the artist responsible for the illustrations to “Britannia Waives the Rules”, The Bystander
In December 1939, the London Opinion published an article about Edward S. Hynes called “They Make us Smile” written by Reginald Arkell], remarking on “his intense sophistication and his accuracy of observation.” Once more it notes that Hynes had no formal training and that his artistic strain was inherited rather than taught.
LESSON FOURTEEN: CARICATURING HUMOROUS DRAWING AND CARTOONING FOR THE BRITISH & DOMINIONS SCHOOL OF DRAWING LTD. LONDON
Hynes was invited to write Lesson Fourteen Caricaturing Humorous Drawing and Cartooning for the British & Dominions School of Drawing Ltd. London. The lesson was part of a correspondence course rather than a physical school and it offered lessons on different types of drawing. The booklets were the “lessons” and students would send their work to the school’s staff for to be assessed. On competition of the course the students would receive a Scholarship Certificate for the British and Dominions School of Drawing.
“A successful caricaturist must be an artist, but it does not at all follow that a successful artist is a caricaturist”. This is how Hynes starts his lesson. He goes on to give advice first about the business side of caricaturing: “you should never draw for publication without remuneration … An artist may not be a businessman, but he must live. He must earn money… If your work is good enough to be printed it is worth paying for”.
The advantages he points out are that the caricaturist can work anywhere, with any medium and does not require “paraphernalia”. He states that “A sense of Humour is essential”, that The line block is most often used for reproduction of caricatures hence the necessity that lines be “firm, distinct and bold”. Practice makes perfect. “It is a very good practice to caricature your friends … keep on pegging away”. “Caricaturing is the very antithesis of photography”, “lines are solid black…let every line be part of the picture…if it is not essential, cut it out” are strong points he makes. “Study your subject first hand…find out what it is that sticks in your memory about people”. “…you must be kind …All the most successful caricaturists have been generous in this respect”. “First and foremost, comes a keen sense of humour, and, secondly, acute observation…I just study them without putting a line in my notebook. Later...I review their features in my mind”. “Hands play a very important part with both actors and politicians. Never ignore them…”. His advice is detailed and full of examples of dos and don’ts and wonderful caricatures to illustrate his words. “Be yourself. Evolve a style of your own” is his advice.
He also gives more generic advice regarding how to approach editors, how to reduce/enlarge pictures depending on the newspaper style and the tools of the craft.
“I portray him as I see him. No caricaturist should seek to do more”.
COCKTAIL CAVALCADE A COMIC PICTURE BOOK FOR GROWN-UPS
In 1937 “Cocktail Cavalcade A Comic Picture Book for Grown-ups” was published, a collection of cartoons with a foreword written by Reginald Arkell (editor of Men Only). By July 1937 he was drawing the covers of Men Only a role he kept to June 1956. Originally Men Only was a pocket magazine with stories, advice, articles, cartoons and photos. Its first issue stated it “did not want women readers”!. His cartoons were also regularly published inside the magazine.
In the 1939 United Kingdom Census his residence was in Lancaster Gate, Paddington, London. He was often photographed with his Morris Cowley car which later accompanied him to Ireland. His artistic talent opened the doors to the high life of London and his work depicting the characters and events of the time decorate pages of the magazines of that era. He eventually moved to a residence in Portman Square, Mayfair.
He was also put forward as Member of the Royal Geographical Society thanks to his having served in the Merchant Navy and under the Royal India Marines as well as a navigating officer. “Has travelled all over the Empire” is the conclusive recommendation.
As Bryant says in his Dictionary of British Cartoonists and Caricaturists 1730-1980[ "Caricatures were enormously popular but public appeal went hand in hand with personal obscurity". The day to day lives of these artists could be glimpsed at through their works but very little was left behind of the men themselves.
Later life
Hynes retired to Bayfield House at Newquay in the Burren. He continued to work with publishers in the UK while painting in oil and charcoal sketches to sell locally. His work can be seen dotted around Ireland in local pubs and hotels.
Eamonn NcNally wrote a retrospective article on Hynes for Clare People on 24 March 2015.  He describes "organised chaos"  on a visit to the artist's studio in the early 1970s where Hynes' paintings, caricatures and the tools of his work lay interspersed with magazines and classical records.
Hynes died in the Burren on 12 May 1982 and is buried at Corocomroe Abbey, Co. Clare.
